messages.author: dae01c57a3c54a3a
messages.subject: Status of boost::math::cyl_bessel_i overflow bug?
parts:
As has been mentioned before, use of the von_mises(mu,kappa) with largish (>10?) values for the kappa parameter tends to yield the exception:

"Exception thrown at line 80: Error in function boost::math::cyl_bessel_i<double>(double,double): numeric overflow"

Now, the solution thus far is to use the fact the fact that as kappa increases, normal(mu,sqrt(1/kappa)) approximates von_mises(mu,kappa) and throw in an if statement using the former when kappa is, say, >10. However, beyond being a bit of a hack, in some circumstances this can cause considerable slowdown. For example, I use the von_mises for mixture data where individual data points get their own value for kappa (well, there's some repetition/grouping, but that's inconsequential here), so I have to do the if-check for every data point. After playing a bit, it seems that when the true value is close to the value used for the if-check, you get dramatically slower performance compared to a version that just uses the von_mises alone. However, in that case sometimes a chain will simply fail to initialize because it hits the exception so frequently.

Obviously getting the underlying boost bug solved would be ideal, but I have no idea what the status of that is (anyone else?). In the interim, one slightly less hacky fix would be to have stan ignore init attempts that fail because of that specific exception. Thoughts?

Oh, and here's some example code (for use from R) demonstrating the timing dramatic difference (there's also a dramatic ESS difference in the same direction):

library(rstan)
library(CircStats) #for rvm
set.seed(1)
y = rvm(1e3,pi,10)

uvm_mod1 = stan_model(model_code=
"
data {
  int N ;
  vector[N] y ;
}
parameters{
  real<lower=0> kappa ;
}
model{
  kappa ~ lognormal(1,1) ;
  for(n in 1:N){
  y[n] ~ von_mises(pi(),kappa) ;
  }
}

"
)

uvm_mod2 = stan_model(model_code=
"
data {
  int N ;
  vector[N] y ;
}
parameters{
  real<lower=0> kappa ;
}
model{
  kappa ~ lognormal(1,1) ;
  for(n in 1:N){
  if(kappa<10){ //use von Mises
  y[n] ~ von_mises(pi(),kappa) ;
  }else{ //use normal approximation
  y[n] ~ normal(pi(),sqrt(1/kappa)) ;
  }
  }
}

"
)


out1 = sampling(
object = uvm_mod1
, data = list(N=length(y),y=y)
, iter = 1e3
, chains = 1
, seed = 1
)

out2 = sampling(
object = uvm_mod2
, data = list(N=length(y),y=y)
, iter = 1e3
, chains = 1
, seed = 1
)

get_elapsed_time(out1)
#I get: chain:1 3.440891 3.652428
get_elapsed_time(out2)
#I get: chain:1 179.3448 183.2809

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: Status of boost::math::cyl_bessel_i overflow bug?
parts:
On Thursday, August 25, 2016 at 8:32:29 PM UTC-4, Mike Lawrence wrote:
As has been mentioned before, use of the von_mises(mu,kappa) with largish (>10?) values for the kappa parameter tends to yield the exception:

"Exception thrown at line 80: Error in function boost::math::cyl_bessel_i<double>(double,double): numeric overflow"

The von_mises function does

log(modified_bessel_first_kind(...

when it should be calculating the logarithm of the BesselI function with log-sum-exp logic. I did this in Stan code for a rstanarm branch

https://github.com/stan-dev/rstanarm/blob/feature/lmList/exec/lm.stan#L90

but it is tedious and would be better if it were a C++ function.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Status of boost::math::cyl_bessel_i overflow bug?
parts:
Mike: any way to keep the values within the computable range?
There's a discussion in the Stan manual for normal approximations for
other ranges which may provide a workaround.

Ben: It looks like Boost doesn't have log-scale versions of their
Bessel functions:

http://www.boost.org/doc/libs/1_61_0/libs/math/doc/html/math_toolkit/bessel/mbessel.html

Are you thinking we'll just take those series expansions
and log them so that it's all log-sum-exp? Makes a lot more
sense than taking the log of the result. These may be
good projects for Thel when she starts in October---all the
original results in the 70s and 80s were from physicists.

Or we could just hack in the workaround discussed in the manual.
Frankly, this math's all beyond me.

- Bob

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Status of boost::math::cyl_bessel_i overflow bug?
parts:
On Thursday, August 25, 2016 at 10:10:21 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
Or we could just hack in the workaround discussed in the manual.
Frankly, this math's all beyond me.

It isn't beyond you. It is just log-sum-exp with an infinite sum so you have to iterate on the log-scale until you find the maximum (presuming it only has one maximum), then keep iterating to find the point where subtracting the maximum results in underflow, then add it all up.

Ben

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Status of boost::math::cyl_bessel_i overflow bug?
parts: That I get.  I meant the Bessel functions themselves and why they show up and how to define new stable numerical algorithms.  Presumably just log-sum-exp-ing the linear approximation algorithm isn't the best approximation to the log of the function for the same reason that autodiffing an iterative algorithm isn't as good as defining a new algorithm.  But like I said, I really don't know.  It also might take a lot of iterations.  Again, I don't know.

parts: Presumably just log-sum-exp-ing the linear approximation algorithm isn't the best approximation to the log of the function for the same reason that autodiffing an iterative algorithm isn't as good as defining a new algorithm.

Yup — we really want to figure out a power series expansion (or asymptotic expansion)
for the log Bessel function directly, which requires a good bit of arcane knowledge.
